title: Outdoor paintings on view indoors at library
text:
A group of artists that paints outdoors is bringing that artwork inside to give the community a glimpse into their plein air perspective.
The gallery from the Plein Air Painters of Narragansett Bay features the artwork of nine Rhode Island painters at the Jamestown Philomenian Library. The group was founded by Natalie Pfanstiehl in 1980. The gallery will be displayed through Sept. 12.
“En plein air” is the French term for “outdoors,” which is where the group paints together every Thursday. They pick a new location somewhere in Rhode Island for each of their meetings, including Jamestown, Newport and Wickford.
Among the current members whose work is displayed is Mary Lou Walter, of Jamestown, who is a retired Scituate art teacher. She said each of the artists paint in their own style, but they share the philosophy of painting outdoors.
“It’s been such a wonderful group of artists,” Walter said. “We encourage one another, we’re always helping one another in many ways, but we’re all individual artists.”
A new perspective
The group was selected to display its work at the library by Jillian Barber, who has curated the library’s exhibits since 1997. While the group has not shown all together at the library before, Walter had her own show there in 2020.
Walter said her favorite parts about being part of the group is being outdoors and discovering new places to paint.
“You think you see, but you really don’t, until you’re drawing out in the breeze, and the sound of the waves and the birds and everything,” Walter said. “When you can just take all of that into your soul and spirit, and it just becomes part of your hand. There’s nothing like it.”
Most of the members, including Walter, were invited by Pfanstiehl after taking lessons with her at the Newport Art Museum. Pfanstiehl, a former newspaper reporter, was a well-known art instructor in Newport who led the plein air group for decades. Pfanstiehl died in 2020 shortly before her 100th birthday, and the group chose not to select a new leader to replace her.
Laura Oakley, of Middletown, who has been with the group for 25 years, said painting en plein air is relaxing. She also enjoys the beauty of the landscapes and seascapes.
“The camaraderie of the group is just fantastic,” Oakley said. “The whole group is very supportive of each other. It’s just a wonderful group to be a part of.”
Oakley, who also is a retired teacher, was invited into the group in 2001 after taking Pfanstiehl’s class. The founder handpicked the members of the group, and among her rules were that they could talk about any subject as long as it was not politics or religion. That rule remains in place today.
The group’s Thursday meetings usually start at about 10 a.m. at their chosen spot of the week, and they end around 1 p.m. to break for lunch. When Pfanstiehl was alive, she would also critique their work and suggest improvements, which Oakley described as helpful and positive. When the weather is inclement, the members meet at the Jamestown library or the Wickford Art Association.
While the members mostly use watercolors, at least one of the members prefers oils and a few others switch between the two mediums. Every artist has a different style. For instance, Walter paints in a realistic style.
Capturing the island
The group has painted several spots in Jamestown throughout the years, including Fort Wetherill, Beavertail State Park, Windmist Farm, Dutch Harbor and The Dumplings. When the group paints in a location, they may not paint in the same spot and instead will find different places in the space they find themselves in that week.
“We’re always choosing different spots,” Walter said. “We go to what talks to us. Sometimes, we sit together and other times, we’re all spread out.”
Some of the artists in the group complete their entire painting outside during one of their weekly sessions, while others take their work home to finish.
Oakley’s personal favorite locale has been The Dumplings, where they painted on a private dock earlier this year. She enjoyed the views of Newport, the boats on the harbor and Clingstone, the famous house on the rock.
Walter said she likes painting by the water: “I love being around the water’s edge and the rocks and the sound of the seagulls. Everything about nature just is wonderful.”
The work from the group that is featured in the library gallery was chosen by the artists themselves. Each artist brought about three or four paintings for consideration. Walter said she chose works that depict Jamestown or the water. Her paintings included Conanicus Avenue, Bristol Harbor and Point Judith Lighthouse near the Fisherman’s Memorial. However, the painting of Conanicus Avenue sold while the show was still hanging, and Walter eventually will replace it.
Oakley’s paintings for the show were completed throughout the summer, and include Windmist Farm, the shack at Dutch Harbor, the Newport Bridge at sunset and the docks at Wickford. The last painting is among her favorites.
‘It just came out with a lot of lightness in the painting,” she said.
Oakley said she hopes visitors to the library take away the “beauty of our area” from their paintings, and how the artists have tried to capture it.

Among the current members whose work is displayed is Mary Lou Walter, of Jamestown, who is a retired Scituate art teacher. The group has painted several spots in Jamestown throughout the years, including Fort Wetherill, Beavertail State Park, Windmist Farm, Dutch Harbor and The Dumplings.
